sources.news_title: Residents in coastal Oregon town urged to evacuate after plant fire
Ammonia tank explodes sending toxic fumes spreading over Oregon town
sources.text:
Residents have been evacuated after a huge fire caused an explosion at a seafood facility this morning.
Footage taken near Pacific Seafood in Newport, Oregon, showed a huge cloud of smoke rising from the plant located near the city’s port on the Yaquina River, home to sea lions.
Locals were told to take cover at an elementary school, before the shelter was moved to a Lutheran Church due to safety concerns relating to ammonia contamination.
All residents within a one-mile radius of the city of around 10,000 people have been asked to leave their homes, with evacuees told they can bring their pets with them.
Shelly Helm, an estate agent, said the incident was ‘heartbreaking’ and that the seafood facility was a large employer in the city, around 130 miles south west of Portland.
The 59-year-old said: ‘It’s a big asset. Hopefully they can rebuild.’
Ammonia is a colourless toxic substance which upon exposure can cause irritation, burns, and damage to the skin, eyes, throat, and lungs.
John Fuller, the public information officer in the city, said it was as of yet unclear what had caused the explosion.
A statement from the local authority said: ‘The City of Newport is evacuating a one-mile radius of Pacific Seafood.
‘A shelter is being set up for evacuees at Sam Case Elementary located at 459 NE 12th St. Evacuees may bring their pets.
‘The evacuation is due to a potential ammonia contamination in the area from the plant.
‘We recommend staying inside if you are in Newport today. If you must go outside, you should wear a mask. Updates will continue to be made on this post.’
Lincoln County Sheriff’s Office added: ‘One important update for those needing the to use the evacuation point, pets are allowed.’
Get in touch with our news team by emailing us at webnews@metro.co.uk.

sources.news_title: DEVELOPING: “GO NOW” Evacuation Ordered After Reported Ammonia Blast at Seafood Plant – 100PercentFedUp.com – by Isaac
sources.text:
A Level 3 “Go Now” evacuation was ordered Sunday in Newport, Oregon, after a major fire tore through a Pacific Seafood processing facility and raised fears of ammonia contamination.
The emergency unfolded along the city’s historic Bayfront, sending thick smoke over the waterfront and forcing residents, workers, and visitors within a wide radius to leave immediately.
Early reports described an ammonia tank explosion inside the seafood plant. Officials have confirmed the fire, the ammonia danger, and the evacuation—but they had not yet publicly established exactly what ignited the blaze or whether a tank itself exploded.
That distinction matters in a fast-moving emergency, but the danger was serious enough for authorities to issue the highest evacuation level.
The Lincoln County Sheriff’s Office said everyone within one mile of 213 SW Bay Boulevard was under a Level 3 order. “Go Now” means leave without delay.
Sam Case Elementary School was initially designated as a temporary evacuation point for people displaced by the emergency.
The sheriff’s notice directed the public to stay clear of the scene and warned people not to call 911 except for life-threatening emergencies. Authorities also closed the western portion of U.S. 20 approaching U.S. 101, limiting access to the Bayfront while fire and hazmat crews worked.
The order expanded beyond the immediate industrial property to cover a full one-mile radius, bringing nearby homes and businesses into the evacuation area. Officials directed residents to Lincoln County’s emergency-alert system for updates rather than attempting to return on their own.
Evacuations are in place within a mile of the Pacific Seafood plant in Newport, Oregon, as firefighters battle a blaze. Authorities warn of potential ammonia contamination in the area. pic.twitter.com/8XqswGoovn
— ABC News (@ABC) October 25, 2026
The evacuation zone covers a substantial part of this small coastal city, including businesses, residences, tourist areas, and sections of the working waterfront.
Newport’s Bayfront is known for its restaurants, shops, fishing fleet, and sea lion docks. Pacific Seafood is also a major local employer, which means the damage could reach far beyond Sunday’s evacuation once the immediate danger has passed.
According to the Lincoln Chronicle, Newport firefighters were dispatched Sunday morning and called for help from departments across Lincoln County. About 40 firefighters were reportedly at the scene by midmorning.
Newport Fire Chief Rob Murphy confirmed that ammonia was present in the smoke, although officials were still determining the concentration and extent of the hazard. A partial roof collapse was also reported inside the plant.
The city urged people elsewhere in Newport to remain indoors. Anyone who had to go outside was advised to wear a mask while emergency crews continued testing and containment work.
Murphy described the response as a long operation rather than a quick knockdown. The Lincoln County School District closed Newport school facilities to the public as a precaution, and smoke seen moving inland added urgency to the evacuation.
Firefighters still had to control the blaze, monitor the air, and determine whether damaged refrigeration equipment continued to pose a hazard.
🇺🇸 | Evacuaciones en Newport, Oregon tras la explosión de un tanque de amoníaco en una planta de procesamiento de mariscos de Pacific Seafood. Se ordenó la evacuación de negocios y viviendas dentro de una milla. No se han reportado heridos hasta el momento. pic.twitter.com/nKqKV3Rjvc
— Centinela 35 (@Centinela_35) October 25, 2026
The good news is that no injuries had been reported in the latest verified updates.
Pacific Seafood said all of its employees were accounted for and that the company was supporting first responders while the incident remained active.
The Associated Press reported that city spokesman John Fuller said the cause of the fire was still unclear. Crews were investigating how much ammonia may have entered the air from chemicals used at the processing plant.
Fuller said the evacuation covered businesses and residences and represented a significant portion of a city with roughly 10,000 residents. The affected Bayfront is both a tourist destination and a working port, with restaurants, shops, fishing operations, and the well-known sea lion docks clustered near the plant.
Witnesses described flames coming from the roof and heavy smoke rising over Yaquina Bay. Pacific Seafood handles processing and distribution across the country, making the facility important to Newport’s waterfront workforce and the wider seafood supply chain.
Ammonia is widely used as an industrial refrigerant, including at food-processing facilities. It has a sharp, recognizable odor, but exposure at high concentrations can become dangerous very quickly.
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention warns that ammonia can injure the eyes, skin, throat, and lungs. Severe exposure can cause breathing difficulty, chemical burns, and potentially life-threatening respiratory damage.
That is why hazmat teams and air monitoring are essential before residents can safely return, even after visible flames and smoke begin to subside.
Ammonia gas is colorless, but its sharp odor can provide an early warning. Odor alone cannot establish whether an area is safe, and people should not move toward the source to investigate.
The danger depends on concentration and duration of exposure, which trained crews measure with specialized equipment. Crews repeat those readings as wind, fire conditions, and the chemical source change.
Children, older adults, and people with existing breathing problems can be especially vulnerable during a chemical-air emergency. The safest course is to follow the evacuation order and wait for measured air-quality results and an official all-clear.
Officials’ stay-inside instruction was designed to reduce contact with smoke while the evacuation zone was cleared. Anyone experiencing significant eye irritation, breathing trouble, chest tightness, or other symptoms after suspected exposure should move away from the contaminated area and seek emergency medical guidance.
NOW: Ammonia tank explodes in Newport, Oregon, area being evacuated pic.twitter.com/X6FP9zShTR
— Miss Mary (@DivintyMary) October 25, 2026
The Gateway Pundit first flagged the developing story and the social-media reports describing an ammonia tank explosion.
The official picture remains more cautious: a major structure fire, possible ammonia contamination, a large evacuation zone, and an investigation into what happened inside the plant.
The outlet reported that hundreds of people were being moved out of the area while firefighters, hazmat teams, and other first responders converged on the waterfront. It also relayed the city’s warning that residents elsewhere in Newport should remain indoors and wear a mask if they had to go outside.
The report correctly emphasized the Level 3 “Go Now” order and the absence of reported injuries. Its tank-explosion description remains a developing claim, however, and should be separated from what authorities have formally confirmed until investigators identify the origin and sequence of the fire.
Residents should rely on Lincoln County emergency alerts and local authorities for changes to evacuation boundaries, shelter locations, road closures, and the eventual all-clear.
This is a developing story and will be updated as officials release additional confirmed information.

sources.news_title: Oregon coastal city issues evacuation order after fire at seafood plant – WTOP News
sources.text:
A coastal city in Oregon issued evacuations after a fire erupted at a seafood wholesaler Sunday morning and there was concern the smoke contained ammonia.
The City of Newport issued the order for a 1-mile (1.6-kilometer) radius around a Pacific Seafood processing plant and set up a shelter at a local church. City officials urged residents and visitors to stay indoors and to wear a mask outside.
John Fuller, the public information officer for the city, told The Associated Press it is not clear what caused the fire. No injuries have been reported, and crews were still at the scene.
Officials were investigating the potential of ammonia contamination in the air due to chemicals at the seafood processing plant, Fuller said.
Ammonia is a colorless gas with a sharp odor. High levels of exposure can cause skin, eye and throat irritation, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
The city, located about 132 miles (212 kilometers) southwest of Portland, Oregon, has a population of about 10,000 people. Its bayfront is a popular tourist attraction featuring restaurants, shops, and tours.
Fuller said the radius includes businesses as well as residences and makes up a “pretty good chunk” of the small town. A shelter originally set up at the Sam Case Elementary School was moved further north away from the plant to the Atonement Lutheran Church as a precaution.
Pacific Seafood is a wholesaler and manufacturer that handles fishing, processing and the distribution of seafood across the country. One of its processing plants sits along the city’s Yaquina Bay, near a dock where sea lions gather.
Shelly Heim was at her home in Newport when she heard sirens and saw smoke coming from the nearby seafood plant. Flames were shooting from the roof, she said.
“It’s heartbreaking,” the 59-year-old real estate agent said, adding that Newport has a strong working port and fishing community and that Pacific Seafood serves as a big place of employment. “It’s a big asset. Hopefully they can rebuild.”
She and her husband didn’t smell anything off in the air and haven’t evacuated, but they were monitoring the wind to make sure it doesn’t change direction and blow the smoke toward them.
Some locals were concerned about the sea lions but they seemed unfazed, Heim said. She took a video of smoke billowing from the plant, and the sea lions could be heard barking as usual.

sources.news_title: Possible ammonia contamination prompts evacuations after Oregon seafood plant fire, officials say
sources.text:
Ammonia contamination after a seafood plant fire prompted recommended evacuations in a coastal Oregon city, local officials said Sunday morning.
The incident occurred at Pacific Seafood in Newport, Oregon, officials said. Thick plumes of smoke billowed over the quiet fishing town Sunday morning, which is located 90 miles southwest of Portland and has just over 10,000 residents.
“We recommend staying inside if you are in Newport today. If you must go outside, you should wear a mask. Updates will continue to be made on this post,” a statement from city officials said.
Officials identified low traces of ammonia in the smoke from the ongoing fire, John Fuller, a city spokesperson, said. There is still a risk with ammonia tanks inside the facility, he added, but did not detail how much material remains.
Hazmat crews were on site to test for air quality levels, he said.
A spokesperson for Pacific Seafood said in a statement the company was not aware of injuries and all employees have been accounted for.
“However, the situation is still ongoing and we are focused on supporting emergency responders to help ensure everyone is safe,” the statement said.
Fuller estimated hundreds of people were in the evacuation area surrounding the processing plant. Officials said the evacuations were strongly recommended but not mandatory.
The Lincoln County Sheriff’s Office said in an afternoon update parts of the recommended evacuation areas in a one-mile radius of the plant were being scaled from evacuation orders to recommendations that residents should be ready to leave if conditions worsen. US 20 from Harney Street West to US 101 is closed, the sheriff’s office said.
An initial half-mile evacuation zone was in the city’s Bayfront area, which is mostly commercial and has some popular tourism areas with fewer homes, Fuller told CNN. The wider evacuation area includes residential areas. It is currently the off season for tourists, he said, though the city still sees some visitors on weekends.
Footage of the scene posted by the city on social media showed firefighters spraying the building down.
City officials had established a shelter for evacuees at a nearby elementary school but changed the location to a Lutheran church further north from the evacuation area out of caution, a city update said Saturday afternoon.
The Oregon State Fire Marshal is responding to the incident with a hazmat team because of chemicals at the facility, the state agency announced in a social media post.
Fire crews were still working on putting out the fire, Fuller said Sunday afternoon. The cause of the fire and ammonia contamination are still under investigation. There are no reported injuries at this time, Fuller confirmed.
Oregon resident Coby Bertalotto shared videos with CNN showing a cloud of smoke over Newport.
“Driving through that thick smoke … It was thick enough that I couldn’t see the side of the road,” Bertalotto said. “I was very cautious.”
He described the smell outside as “rubbery,” affecting an area with several tourist attractions such as candy stores, bars and Ripley’s Believe It or Not.
“There are probably about three or four blocks that are just getting smoked out,” Bertalotto said.
Exposure to high levels of ammonia in the air may cause irritation to the skin, eyes, throat, and lungs and cause coughing and burns, according to the Agency for Toxic Substances and Disease Registry. Some people with asthma may be more sensitive, the agency said.
This story has been updated with additional information.
CNN’s Nic F. Anderson and Maria Aguilar Prieto contributed to this report.

sources.news_title: Evacuation ordered in Newport for ammonia after Pacific Seafood fire
Evacuations issued along Newport bayfront due to fire at Pacific Seafood
sources.text:
Residents and businesses within a mile of the Newport Bayfront were asked to evacuate Sunday after a large fire and ammonia leak at one of Pacific Seafood’s plants threatened the commercial and tourist-oriented area along Yaquina Bay.
Firefighters from departments from throughout Lincoln County have been pouring water on the plant at 245 S.E. Bay Blvd. since the first alarm at 8:51 a.m. Sunday.
As of early Sunday there were 40 firefighters and a special Oregon State Fire Marshal’s hazardous material response team at the scene. Police blocked entrances to the Bayfront.
Smoke billowed out of Pacific Seafoods, enveloping the hills to the north. Smoke could be smelled throughout the city including outside of Sam Case Elementary, which was initially set up as an evacuation center. The center was later moved to Atonement Lutheran Church along U.S. Highway 101.
The city put emergency procedures into place and ordered evacuations of homes and businesses within a mile of the plant – including all Port of Newport facilities, its RV park and marina on the south side of Yaquina Bay. The Hatfield Marine Science Center also closed. Businesses shuttered for the day.
Newport fire chief Rob Murphy confirmed that there was ammonia in the smoke from the fire but was unsure to what degree. It was the acrid smoke and threat from the ammonia that prompted the evacuation notice.
“It’s going to be a long operation,” Murphy told the Lincoln Chronicle.
No injuries have been reported.
The Oregon State Fire Marshal sent a regional hazardous materials team and coordinator to Newport to help.
A spokesman for Clackamas-based Pacific Seafood said in a statement to the Lincoln Chronicle they were not aware of any injuries and all employees were accounted for.
“However, the situation is still ongoing and we are focused on supporting emergency responders to help ensure everyone is safe,” the statement said. “We will work closely with appropriate authorities to understand the circumstances surrounding the incident once the immediate response is complete.”
By 11:45 a.m. Sunday about a dozen evacuees, many with pets, had come to the elementary school where district employees had set up food and water. That number rose to 25-30 by the time the shelter operation was moved to the church.
No injuries have been reported.
The Oregon State Fire Marshal said it was sending a regional hazardous materials team and coordinator to Newport to help.
Smoke billowed out of Pacific Seafoods and enveloped the hill on Hatfield Drive, where police blocked an entrance to the Bayfront. Residents could smell smoke throughout the city including outside of Sam Case Elementary.
Because of the threat of ammonia contamination, the city recommended that Newport residents stay inside Sunday or if they go outside to wear a mask.
The city set up a gathering area for anyone evacuated from the area at Sam Case Elementary School.
Caitlin Ryan, who lives on Lee Street directly north of the plant, was in her pajamas in bed when she got the evacuation order. She quickly rounded up her two children and their dog, jumped into their car and headed to the school.
“I’m just very nervous, I couldn’t get my kitten to cooperate and had to leave other pets at home,” Ryan said.
Marsha and Dave Eckleman live by the Newport Recreation Center and first found out about the fire when a neighbor called them at 9:35 a.m. The took only their phones and keys with them when they were evacuated.
“We’d rather be home but ammonia is no joke,” Dave Eckleman said.

sources.news_title: Level 3 evacuation issued near Newport Bayfront due to fire
sources.text:
Fire contained at Pacific Seafood blaze; evacuations remain over potential ammonia threat
NEWPORT, Ore — Multiple agencies are on scene of a large structure fire at the Pacific Seafood facility on Newport's historic Bayfront, prompting a significant emergency response.
The Lincoln County Sheriff's Office issued level 2 and 3 evacuations within a mile of the facility, located at 203 SW Bay Boulevard.
An evacuation shelter has been moved to Atonement Lutheran Church at 2315 N Coast Hwy. Residents are allowed to bring their pets there as well. According to the city of Newport, the evacuation is due to potential ammonia contamination. The city also recommends that people stay indoors today. It is recommended that you wear a mask if you do need to go outdoors today in Newport.
People in the evacuation area should leave immediately. Officials ask the public to call 911 only for life-threatening emergencies.
Oregon State Fire Marshal Mariana Ruiz-Temple said crews first got the call about the fire at 8:30 a.m., prompting her agency to mobilize a state hazmat team over concerns about an anhydrous ammonia tank on-site, a potentially dangerous chemical used for refrigeration, but no ammonia leak has been confirmed.
“Thankfully, we have not received any notion that we have a leak at this time.” She explained that although ammonia is common, “it also is a very dangerous gas,” noting its potential to irritate skin, eyes and lungs if released.
Firefighters managed to contain the fire, making sure it did not spread to other businesses.
The main risk to the tanks, Ruiz-Temple said, has been the possibility of a structural collapse caused by the ongoing efforts to put out the fire. “The concern would be that if that does occur over the tank itself or near the tank and it punctures that could cause the release and so that is our number one concern,” she said. At last check, officials did not believe any tank had ruptured.
Additional fire service resources are heading to Newport to support local crews through the night and into Monday. The State Fire Marshal’s office confirmed that a strike team from Lane County would arrive in the morning and a Marion County task force would bring extra engines and a ladder truck to ease the burden on exhausted firefighters.
“We have additional fire resources coming in through the evening and we’re maintaining our state hazmat teams to do that plume modeling as necessary and air monitoring as well,” Ruiz-Temple said.
According to the city of Newport, there have been no reported injuries at this time, but one firefighter was sent to the hospital for exhaustion Ruiz-Temple said. There is no official cause for what started the fire.
Gov. Kotek put out a statement on X saying, "we are closely monitoring the fire at Pacific Seafood in Newport. Thank you to the first responders working tirelessly to protect lives and property. The state will continue to provide all resources necessary to support local fire teams on the ground".
Pacific Seafood provided KATU with this statement about the situation at their business. "At this time, we are not aware of any reported injuries, and all of our team members are accounted for. However, the situation is still ongoing, and we are focused on supporting emergency responders to help ensure everyone is safe. We are incredibly grateful for and actively working with first responders to make sure everything is handled with the necessary caution and care. We will work closely with appropriate authorities to understand the circumstances surrounding the incident once the immediate response is complete. We appreciate the efforts and cooperation of everyone in Newport".
According to the Lincoln County Sheriff's Office, Samaritan Pacific Communities Hospital is operating as normal.
The Sheriff’s Office said updates will be posted at LINCALERTS. The notice was posted at 10:13 a.m. Sunday, October 25.

sources.news_title: Newport Orders One-Mile Evacuation Zone After Fire at Pacific Seafood Facility
sources.text:
NEWPORT, Ore. (Oct. 25, 2026)— Emergency evacuations were ordered for much of Newport’s historic Bayfront on Sunday morning after a reported fire at a Pacific Seafood facility raised concerns about possible ammonia contamination.
According to the Lincoln County Sheriff’s Office, emergency personnel responded at approximately 10:13 a.m. to reports of a possible fire at the Pacific Seafood plant, located at 213 SW Bay Blvd.
By 10:34 a.m., the city of Newport announced an immediate evacuation of a one-mile radius surrounding the facility due to concerns about potential ammonia contamination in the area.
The evacuation order affected much of Newport’s Bayfront district, prompting officials to direct residents and others in the affected area to leave immediately.
City officials designated Sam Case Elementary School, located at 459 NE 12th St., as a gathering location for evacuees. Residents were advised that pets would be permitted at the location.
In addition to the evacuation order, officials recommended that people in Newport remain indoors and wear a mask if they must go outside.
Ammonia is commonly used as a refrigerant in seafood processing facilities. Exposure to elevated concentrations can cause respiratory irritation and other potentially serious health effects.
As of Sunday morning, authorities had not released additional information about the extent of the fire, whether ammonia had been released or whether any injuries had occurred.
The cause of the reported fire also remained unknown.
Officials have not announced when evacuated residents and businesses will be allowed to return.
Gov Kotek released the following statement:
We are closely monitoring the fire at Pacific Seafood in Newport.
Thank you to the first responders working tirelessly to protect lives and property. The state will continue to provide all resources necessary to support local fire teams on the ground.
Medford Alert News will continue to monitor this incident and provide updates as new and confirmed information becomes available.
